Upper bounds — holds for every partial

  • \(\mathrm{MAdv}(f) = O\big(\mathrm{Q}_{\varepsilon}(f)\big)\)
    Spalek08
    It is a lower-bound method for $\mathrm{Q}$, so it cannot exceed it.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{MAdv}(f) = \Omega\big(\mathrm{Q}_{\varepsilon}(f)\big)\)
    Spalek08 Reichardt11
    Via $\mathrm{Adv}^{\pm} \le \mathrm{MAdv}$ below and $\mathrm{Adv}^{\pm} = \Theta(\mathrm{Q}_\varepsilon)$.

So as a number the multiplicative adversary tells you nothing that \(\mathrm{Adv}^{\pm}(f)\) does not. What it buys is the regime: the multiplicative progress measure survives success probability $2^{-\Omega(T)}$, which is what strong direct product theorems need, whereas the additive bound degrades to nothing once the success probability drops below a constant. Every value on a function page is therefore recorded as $\Theta(\mathrm{Q})$ and derived.

see also: \(\mathrm{Adv}^{\pm}(f)\), \(\mathrm{Q}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{Adv}(f)\) data/relations/03-quantum.yaml

A single character has sparsity $1$ and $\mathrm{osss} = 1$: the two agree, but neither
grows, so this witnesses no exponent. No function in the zoo has $\mathrm{osss}$ growing
while $\mathrm{spar}$ stays bounded -- indeed $\mathrm{spar}(f) = O(1)$ forces $f$ to be a
constant-size combination of characters, and $\mathrm{osss}$ is then bounded too.
